title: Mozambique Approves Exxon’s Redesigned $30 Billion Rovuma LNG Plan | OilPrice.com
text:
Thiel Doubles Down on Vaca Muerta as Trump Calls Venezuela an “Acquisition”

Mozambique’s Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved ExxonMobil’s (NYSE:XOM) amended development plan for the Rovuma LNG project, clearing a regulatory hurdle before a final investment decision (FID) the company expects by the end of the year. The government said the revised plan lowers development costs through electric natural gas processing modules, O Económico reported.

The amended plan raises the onshore plant’s capacity to 18.6 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), from the 15.2 mtpa approved in 2019, Bloomberg reported. Standard Bank estimates the project could cost nearly $30 billion, which would make it Mozambique’s largest onshore development.

Mozambique’s National Petroleum Institute (INP) expects the redesign to cut emissions by around 40%. It estimates the state could receive around $121 billion over the plant’s 25-year production life, The Energy Year reported. The plan reserves 25% of the gas produced for Mozambique’s domestic market.

ExxonMobil agreed in October to raise its stake in Rovuma LNG to 50% through an asset swap with Eni (NYSE:E), which will concentrate on floating LNG developments in Area 4 of the Rovuma Basin, including Coral Sul and Coral Norte. Dan Ammann, president of ExxonMobil’s upstream business, met President Daniel Chapo in Maputo on Monday, The Rio Times reported. Bloomberg reported that output could start in the early 2030s.

A TotalEnergies-led (NYSE:TTE) group formally resumed work this year on the adjacent $20 billion Mozambique LNG project, which has a capacity of 13.1 mtpa. Insurgent attacks in Cabo Delgado province had forced workers to evacuate and delayed both onshore projects for years. BloombergNEF says the projects planned in Mozambique would lift the country’s LNG capacity to nearly 45 mtpa, about 10% of global supply last year.

Supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have increased interest in alternative sources of LNG, and BloombergNEF expects global LNG demand to rise about 40% in the decade through 2035. Fitch forecasts that sub-Saharan Africa’s LNG exports will rise by nearly 175% to 98 billion cubic meters by 2034, from 35.7 billion cubic meters in 2024.
